title: Google's AI genome system evaluates every possible one-base change
content:
On Tuesday, Google announced AlphaGenome Atlas, a resource that attempts to predict the consequences of every possible single-base variant in the human genome. The human genome is about 3 billion bases long, so trying the other three DNA bases that don’t appear in our reference genome means sending a total of 9 billion bases through AlphaGenome software.
AlphaGenome is designed to identify potential functions of non-coding DNA, which does not encode proteins but makes up the vast majority of the human genome. Some of this non-coding DNA is essential for controlling the activity of the protein-coding portion—it tells the cell where and when to make messenger RNAs, how to process them into mature protein-coding forms, and so on. But much of it appears to be little more than the remains of viruses and other molecular parasites.
Being able to identify the functional portion is very useful, as is having all the analysis done by a single software package. But until biologists start to use it heavily (assuming they do), it won’t be clear what AlphaGenome offers beyond what we could have gotten out of its training data.
Non-coding sequences
While we tend to focus on proteins, the portion of the human genome that encodes proteins is less than 3 percent. Most of the genome is non-coding and contains a mix of things, including centromeres, which help ensure chromosomes are divided evenly between cells, and caps that protect the chromosome ends. There’s also the regulatory DNA that controls gene activity, along with the signals that help determine what should and shouldn’t be included in mature messenger RNAs produced by genes. Other sequences help control how the DNA is packaged inside the cell.

report.summary: Google announced AlphaGenome Atlas, an AI system that predicts functional consequences for all 9 billion possible single-base human genome variants.
report.background: About 97% of the human genome is non-coding, meaning it does not directly produce proteins. Within this non-coding expanse are regulatory sequences that control when and where genes are activated, as well as structural elements like centromeres and telomeres. Much of the rest is made up of leftover viral fragments and other molecular parasites. Despite its importance, non-coding DNA is poorly understood, and interpreting variants there remains a major challenge. AlphaGenome is Google's attempt to use deep learning to assign function or consequence to these non-coding regions by scoring every possible single-base change in the human genome. This creates a comprehensive atlas of potential genetic effects, filling a gap left by tools focused mainly on protein-coding mutations.
key_points: The Atlas evaluates 9 billion single-base changes: for each of the roughly 3 billion positions in the human reference genome, it tests the three alternative DNA bases, producing a complete annotation of possible point variants. This scale gives researchers a systematic view of non-coding variation.

Less than 3 percent of the human genome codes for proteins; the rest is non-coding, including enhancers, promoters, splicing signals, and structural elements. AlphaGenome specializes in these non-coding regions, which are often overlooked by traditional variant predictors.

AlphaGenome's AI predicts whether a mutation will disrupt regulatory functions, such as turning genes on or off, splicing messenger RNA, or packaging DNA inside cells. That helps distinguish harmful variants from neutral ones without requiring expensive experimental tests.

The most meaningful test will come from real use: because AlphaGenome was trained on existing genomic annotations, its findings may largely reflect what was already known. Whether it discovers genuinely novel regulatory mechanisms is uncertain until biologists validate its predictions experimentally.

Google positions this as a public resource for the genetics community, potentially aiding diagnosis of developmental disorders, cancer research, or personalized medicine. However, its ultimate value depends on the atlas's usability and whether it gains broad adoption among clinical and research labs.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AlphaGenome reinforces deep learning's expanding role in interpreting biological sequence data, with Google pushing beyond protein structure into whole-genome regulatory function. For researchers, it could dramatically reduce the time spent hypothesizing about non-coding variants, allowing them to prioritize experiments on mutations most likely to matter. For genetic counselors and clinicians, comprehensive variant effect scores might eventually aid in interpreting whole-genome sequences when patients have no obvious protein-coding mutations. Regular users may indirectly benefit as diagnostic yield improves, though broad clinical use remains far off. Developers and data scientists can build follow-up models to refine predictions, but the field will need independent benchmarks and experimental validation before AlphaGenome becomes a standard tool.
report.tools: Researchers interested in comparing variant effects can explore Google's AlphaGenome Atlas once accessible, and watch for DeepMind's public datasets. Complementary open-source tools include Ensembl VEP for annotating genomic variants, gnomAD for population frequency data, and IGV for visualizing genomic context. For deep-learning experimentation, tools like Kipoi and torchomics offer model hubs for DNA sequence models.
